items.title: What the Civil Service is (level 1)
items.body: The Civil Service is the group of people who work for the government and help it run the country. People who work in it are called civil servants. They are not politicians. Ministers are the politicians who lead government departments. The Prime Minister chooses them, and they are usually Members of Parliament (MPs) or members of the House of Lords. Ministers decide what the government wants to do. This is called policy. Civil servants give ministers advice and then carry out the decisions that are made. When a general election brings in a new government, the ministers change but the civil servants stay in their jobs. Civil servants are paid from public money, which mostly comes from taxes paid by people and businesses. The Civil Service does many everyday jobs: paying benefits and pensions, collecting tax, issuing passports and driving licences, and running prisons and supporting courts. Around half a million people work in the Civil Service. They work in towns and cities all over the UK, not only in London. Teachers in state schools, NHS nurses and council bin collectors are public sector workers, but they are not civil servants. The Civil Service is non-political: it works for whichever government is in power.

items.title: The four Civil Service values (level 1)
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out the standards that every civil servant is expected to meet. It is built on four core values. The first is integrity. This means putting the duty of public service above your own interests and not misusing your position. The second is honesty. This means being truthful and open, and not misleading anyone. The third is objectivity. This means basing your advice and decisions on careful analysis of the evidence, not on personal opinion. The fourth is impartiality. This means acting only on the merits of the case and serving equally well governments of different political parties. Together these four values help the public trust the Civil Service. The Code is part of every civil servant's terms of appointment, so it applies to everyone from the newest Administrative Assistant to the most senior official. You can read the Civil Service Code on GOV.UK. Many job adverts and interviews refer to it, so a candidate who knows the four values is better prepared. The values are sometimes shortened to the letters I, H, O and I. If you are asked to do something that conflicts with the Code, you should say so and raise it with a manager.

items.title: Government departments and what they do (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies
items.body: Government departments are the large organisations that carry out the work of government. Each one covers a particular area. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) pays benefits and the State Pension and runs Jobcentre Plus. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) collects taxes and pays some support such as Child Benefit. The Home Office deals with immigration, passports, policing policy and national security. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) is responsible for courts, prisons and probation in England and Wales. The Department for Education (DfE) is responsible for schools and children's services in England. The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) is responsible for health and adult social care in England. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is responsible for the armed forces and defence. The Department for Transport (DfT) is responsible for roads, railways and aviation policy. HM Treasury looks after the government's money and sets tax and spending plans. The Cabinet Office supports the Prime Minister and helps different departments work together. Each department is led by a minister, usually called a Secretary of State, and the most senior civil servant in a department is called the Permanent Secretary. Departments have offices in many places, so you may find a job near you.

items.title: Agencies and other public bodies (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies
items.body: Many departments have agencies attached to them. An agency usually does a particular job and has its own staff, though it still belongs to its parent department. The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) keeps records of drivers and vehicles, issues driving licences and collects vehicle tax. It is part of the Department for Transport. HM Passport Office issues passports and is part of the Home Office. The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) runs driving tests and checks vehicle safety, and is also part of the Department for Transport. His Majesty's Prison and Probation Service (HMPPS) runs prisons and probation in England and Wales, as part of the Ministry of Justice. HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS) runs the courts and tribunals, also as part of the Ministry of Justice. HM Land Registry records who owns land and property in England and Wales. Companies House keeps the official record of companies in the UK. There are also public bodies that work at arm's length from government, such as the Environment Agency. When you search for a job on Civil Service Jobs, you will see departments and agencies listed as the employer, and you can search by either.

items.title: The civil service grades (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service grades; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Civil Service jobs are arranged in grades. A grade shows how senior a job is and how much responsibility it carries. From the bottom, the main grades are: Administrative Assistant (AA), Administrative Officer (AO), Executive Officer (EO), Higher Executive Officer (HEO), Senior Executive Officer (SEO), Grade 7 and Grade 6. Above these is the Senior Civil Service (SCS), which is the group of the most senior civil servants. Administrative Assistant and Administrative Officer are the two lowest grades, and they are the usual starting points for people who join without a Civil Service background. Many AA and AO adverts do not ask for formal qualifications. The next grade up is Executive Officer. People often apply for a higher grade after they have gained experience. Each advert on Civil Service Jobs states its grade, so you can see at a glance whether a job is at AO level or higher. Grades are used in all departments, although job titles may differ. Pay is set for each grade by the department, so an AO in one department may be paid slightly differently from an AO in another. The advert always shows the salary for that role.

items.title: The Administrative Officer role (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Civil Service grades
items.body: The Administrative Officer (AO) is an entry-level job in the Civil Service. AOs do the practical, everyday work that keeps a department running. In many departments this means working with the public. An AO might answer phone calls, reply to letters and emails, check forms and documents, enter information onto computer systems, process benefit or tax claims, or book appointments. In other places an AO works in an office team, keeping records, sorting post, preparing papers and helping managers. The work needs accuracy, because small mistakes in a record can cause big problems for a person. It also needs good communication, because AOs often explain things to people who are worried or confused. AOs usually work under a line manager, who is the person who gives them work, supports them and reviews how they are doing. New staff are given training for the systems and rules they need. Many AO jobs are full time, but part-time and flexible working are often available. People who work well as AOs can move up to Executive Officer. You do not usually need a degree or any exam passes to apply for an AO role, but you will need to show the skills and behaviours listed in the advert.

items.title: Where Civil Service jobs are (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Civil Service jobs are found in every part of the UK. Many people think they are all in London, but most civil servants work outside the capital. Large departments such as DWP and HMRC have offices in towns and cities across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The DVLA is based in Swansea in Wales. Government departments have large offices in places such as Newcastle, Leeds, Manchester, Birmingham, Glasgow, Cardiff and Belfast, as well as London. This means you can often find a job close to where you live. Some roles are advertised as hybrid, which means you spend part of the week in the office and part working from home. Others need you to be in the office all the time, for example where you handle paper documents or sensitive information. Northern Ireland has its own Civil Service, called the Northern Ireland Civil Service. The Scottish Government and the Welsh Government employ civil servants too. On Civil Service Jobs you can search by location, so you can filter for jobs in your area. Always read the location in the advert, because some jobs can be done in more than one place.

items.title: Types of work in the Civil Service (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service functions and professions; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: The Civil Service has many different kinds of job, which are grouped into functions and professions. The biggest group is operational delivery. These are the people who deal directly with the public and run services: they answer calls and letters, process claims and check cases. Jobs at AA and AO level are often in operational delivery. Policy is the group that works with ministers on advice and new ideas. Digital and data staff build and run websites and computer systems and look after information. Finance staff manage budgets and check spending. Human resources (HR) staff look after recruitment, pay and support for employees. Communications staff share information with the public and the press. Project delivery staff plan and manage projects such as new buildings or IT systems. Legal staff, economists, statisticians and scientists also work in the Civil Service. Each advert on Civil Service Jobs says which profession the job belongs to. If you want to move between professions later, you can, and training is often offered. Knowing which group a job belongs to helps you understand what the work will be like.

items.title: Civil Service Jobs and applying (level 1)
items.body: Most Civil Service vacancies are advertised on one website called Civil Service Jobs. You can use it for free. To apply you first create an account. You then fill in your profile with your personal details, and the website keeps them so you do not have to type them again for each application. You can search for jobs by location, grade, department and salary. You can also save your search and switch on job alerts, so the site emails you when a new job matches. Each advert has a closing date and time, and late applications are not accepted. The advert explains how you will be assessed, which could be a form, a personal statement, an online test or an interview. The first step after you apply is called a sift, where recruiters check your application against the criteria. If you are offered a job, the offer is conditional on pre-employment checks, such as proof of identity and right to work. Applying never costs money, and nobody should ask you to pay to apply. If you need help to apply, for example because of a disability, the advert gives a contact for reasonable adjustments.

items.title: Key government words (level 1)
items.source: UK Parliament; GOV.UK, How government works
items.body: A few words come up again and again when you read about the Civil Service. Parliament is the place where laws are debated and made. It has two parts: the House of Commons, whose members are elected MPs, and the House of Lords. The government is the group of ministers, led by the Prime Minister, who run the country on a day-to-day basis. The Prime Minister is the head of the government. The Cabinet is a group of the most senior ministers who meet regularly to make big decisions. A general election is the vote in which people choose MPs; the party that can command a majority in the House of Commons usually forms the government. A manifesto is a document in which a party explains what it will do if it wins. A bill is a proposed new law. When Parliament agrees it, it becomes an Act. Legislation is the general word for laws. The Opposition is the largest party that is not in government. Civil servants do not belong to any of these political groups. They work for the government of the day and support the ministers who lead their department, whichever party is in power.

items.title: Public money and keeping things private (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Code; GOV.UK; Information Commissioner's Office
items.body: Civil servants work with public money and with private information, and both need care. Public money is money that comes from taxpayers. Civil servants must use it properly and not waste it. HM Treasury is the department that sets the government's spending plans and checks that departments spend public money wisely. The National Audit Office (NAO) is an independent body that checks how departments have spent their money and reports to Parliament. Many civil servants also see private information about people, such as names, addresses, income, health or family details. This is personal data. The law, including the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, says it must be kept safe and used only for the right reasons. Civil servants should only look at a person's records when their job requires it. Looking at the record of a friend, relative or neighbour out of curiosity is wrong and can lead to disciplinary action. Official information that has not been published should not be shared outside work. This duty of confidentiality continues even after you leave the Civil Service. If you are not sure whether you can share something, ask your line manager first.

items.title: Fair recruitment and the Civil Service Commission (level 1)
items.body: Civil Service jobs are filled fairly. The rule is that people are chosen on merit, in fair and open competition. Merit means the person who best meets the criteria for the job gets it. It does not depend on who you know, your background or your political views. Anyone who is eligible can apply. The Civil Service Commission is an independent body that makes sure recruitment follows these rules. It publishes the Recruitment Principles. Independent means it is separate from ministers and departments, so it can check them without being told what to say. The Commission also hears complaints from civil servants who think the Civil Service Code has been broken and have been unable to resolve the matter inside their department. Applicants with a disability can ask for reasonable adjustments, such as extra time in a test or a different format of document. The Disability Confident scheme offers an interview to disabled applicants who meet the minimum requirements of the job. Asking for an adjustment does not count against you. The Civil Service wants staff who reflect the whole country, and it welcomes applications from people of all backgrounds, ages and abilities.

items.title: People you will hear about at work (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service structure; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: When you join the Civil Service you will hear a few job titles used for people in your department. A customer or claimant is a member of the public who uses a service, for example someone claiming a benefit or applying for a passport. Your line manager is the person who directs your daily work. Your team leader or Executive Officer may be your first line manager in an operational team. A caseworker deals with individual cases, such as an application or a claim, from start to finish. A case is the file or record about one person's application. A caseload is the number of cases one person is looking after at a time. A minister leads the department and is a politician. A Private Office is a small team of civil servants who support a minister and manage their diary and paperwork. The Permanent Secretary is the most senior civil servant and runs the department day to day. Some staff are called policy advisers, and they work with ministers on new ideas. Your department will also have a human resources team, called HR, who help with pay, leave and any problems at work. Knowing who does what helps you ask the right person.

items.title: Pay, leave and pensions (level 1)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Civil Service pensions
items.body: When you read a Civil Service advert, the salary is stated clearly. Pay depends on the grade, the department and sometimes the location, so a job in London may pay more than the same grade elsewhere. The advert may give a range rather than a single figure. Civil servants are paid monthly into their bank account. Most civil servants can join the Civil Service pension scheme, which pays an income when you retire. The scheme that new joiners normally join is called Alpha. Both you and your employer pay into it. Civil servants also receive paid annual leave, which is the number of days off a year you are paid for, and they are paid when they are off sick, within the department's rules. Public holidays are in addition to annual leave in many departments. Many jobs offer flexible working, which means some choice about the hours you work or where you work. Full details are in the advert and in your contract. Take time to read both before you accept, and do not guess. If something is not clear, you can ask the contact named in the advert or the HR team once you have an offer.

items.title: Learning and moving up (level 1)
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service Learning; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: The Civil Service wants staff to keep learning. When you join you will have an induction, which is a first few days of training and introductions. You will complete mandatory learning, which is training every civil servant must do, for example on security, data protection and equality. After that you can use training courses and online learning to build your skills. A one-to-one is a regular meeting with your line manager to talk about your work, your progress and any help you need. An objective is a goal you agree with your manager. Many people move up the grades during their career. To be promoted you usually apply for a job at the next grade, either in your own department or in another one. Some departments offer apprenticeships, which combine paid work with study for a qualification, and these can be a good route if you have no formal qualifications. A mentor is an experienced person who gives you advice and support. A buddy is a colleague who helps you settle in during your first weeks. Moving up is normal in the Civil Service, and people often apply for the next grade after a year or two of experience.
